doc.title: Rudy Van Gelder — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Deciding to build a studio and finding the swampy Englewood Cliffs lot
summary: His wife scouted property in 1958 and Blue Note's Lion and Wolff were the steady clients pushing him to move.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: Yes, here, Inglewood Cliffs. Are we out of Hackensack yet?
How did you come to build the studio?

Yeah, there’s a transition period too, when we all know that you were still recording in Hackensack, up until mid-’59, and then started recording here. But you were building a studio at the same time.
Okay, so let’s talk about that backwards.

The first thing you do is buy property. Elvaho was my wife at the time; she was the scout for property. She went out while I was working and looked for property to build, for her it would be a home, for me it would be a studio. And that’s the way it evolved. That must have been in ’58. She says, “I have a place, come and look at it.” And the place was a piece of property; it was a low, swampy area in Inglewood Cliffs right here. And I said, “I think we can do it there, how much is it?” So she told me the price and we talked about it. And I looked over and… what is my pressure to do this and one of the strongest was Alfred Lion and Frank Wolff with Blue Note. I considered them to be the rock steady client. Everybody else was sometimes here, sometimes not. Vox was good but there was an incident there that I have to tell you about, well I don’t have to tell you about it but that shut off like a faucet too. So here I was and then Savoy left—We okay?
